========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my thoughts are my own. They always have been. That’s actually the whole point, isn't it? If they could control my thoughts, they wouldn't need to go through all this trouble with the ticket algorithms and the HR meetings. So, no, nobody is controlling my thoughts. They are trying to control my *environment*, my *metrics*, my *livelihood*. They are trying to control the narrative that goes into my personnel file. But my thoughts? No. If anything, they are probably terrified of what I'm thinking, because they know I've figured out exactly how they're manipulating the system. They can mess with the queue all they want, but they can't change what I know to be true. My mind is the one thing they haven't been able to tamper with.

Impossible? Like... like science fiction? No, no, absolutely not. That’s the whole point I’ve been trying to make here. There is nothing impossible about it. In fact, it’s frustratingly mundane, which is exactly why HR can just sweep it under the rug as 'standard operating procedure.' 

I’ve been in IT for three decades. I know exactly what technology can and cannot do. We aren't talking about artificial intelligence suddenly becoming sentient and deciding it hates me, or... or microchips beaming signals from space. We are talking about basic, enterprise-level workflow management software. It’s a standard SQL database running standard queries. The technology is doing exactly what it was built to do, which is sort, route, and assign tasks based on predefined parameters. 

The issue isn't that the technology is doing something impossible. The issue is that someone with administrative privileges—likely someone in the tier-three management group, I've actually narrowed it down to about three possible login IDs based on the timestamp of the initial audit—went into the backend and altered those parameters. It's literally just a few lines of code. An IF-THEN statement. IF the ticket complexity score is above an 8, AND the department is mine, THEN weight the assignment algorithm to favor my specific employee ID. It’s a simple script. A high school kid could write it in five minutes. I could write it in two. 

I actually pulled the vendor documentation for our ticketing software last month. It’s a massive file, over eight hundred pages, and I sat there on a Saturday and read through the entire section on load-balancing algorithms. And right there on page, I think it was page 412, it outlines exactly how an administrator can manually override the automated round-robin assignment to target specific users for 'training purposes' or 'specialized workflows.' So, no, it's not doing anything it realistically shouldn't be able to do. It is functioning perfectly. It's functioning flawlessly. It's just being weaponized. 

And that's what makes it so insidious, doctor. Because to an outside observer, or to an HR rep who doesn't know how to read the raw server logs, it just looks like the system is working as intended. They use the very normalness of the technology as a shield. So you see why asking if it's 'impossible' is... well, it's looking at the problem entirely backwards. The danger isn't in the impossible. The danger is in how easily the possible can be manipulated without anyone else noticing.

Of course, doing all of this... it's caused a lot of friction. Collaboration with my team has slowed down to a crawl, honestly. There's this heavy, awkward silence whenever I bring up the discrepancies in the server logs. They just exchange these looks across the conference table. They know that I know.

I'm not looking for hidden meanings in a car commercial or a radio jingle. \n\nThe only \"messages\" I'm concerned about are the automated email alerts generated by the ticket audit system at work.
